title: Citational Politics and Practices in Viking Age Archaeology and Beyond
text:
Monday April 13 – Tuesday April 14, 2026
University of Oslo
Poster PDF | Poster HTML
BibVik is a bibliometric study that aims to discover different threads and tendencies regarding how Viking Age archaeological research are pursued. It takes a critical, feminist and reflexive stance on research practice and on how research practice can be documented and analyzed.
We are not alone in this approach. Although archaeologists and others in the domain of Nordic cultural heritage are increasingly engaged in research on research practice, the work sometimes feel scattered or tangential to archaeologists’ primary research interests. This workshop therefore assemble a community of like-minded scholars who have not only done comprehensive and digitally-mediated archaeological meta-research rooted in bibliometric methods, but who have done so from a critical and feminist perspective.
The purpose of the workshop is twofold:

title: Citational Politics and Practices in Viking Age Archaeology and Beyond
text:
Guiding Questions
Each presentation slot is 25 minutes, which includes time for questions directed to the speakers. Time is also reserved for breaking out into focused group discussions and for structured plenary discussion at the end of each day.
Discussion may focus on the following themes:

How can bibliometric, meta-research, and digital approaches in general be leveraged to produce or assist with feminist, anti-colonial, or other forms of reflexive critique within archaeology?
What methodological challenges (including those relating to data availability and quality) exist, and how might we overcome them?
What are the limits of bibliometric approaches, what voices do they exclude, and how might we better account for missing or under-represented perspectives?
What specific considerations should be made when applying these approaches in the context of Viking Age archaeology and in other distinct subdisciplines, domains or areas of interest?
How do we establish supportive referential practices in archaeological research, and avoid closed networks, and how may bibliometric studies contribute to this process?

Participants are welcome to access and contribute to a shared notes file.

title: Discussion Topics
text:
Developing the codebook
Julie worked on it with another colleague (I don’t recall his name). We discussed means of improving it further. Specifically: develop groupings, and highlighting or boldening terms that stand out as the core concept or heading.
We also clarified how this is an iterative process. The codes are not meant to be prescriptive, and should adapt to reflect the contents of the corpus and the realizations we make as coding progresses.

title: Discussion Topics
section: Assessing the quality of scholarly metadata
text:
Assessing the quality of scholarly metadata
Zack looked into the quality of scholarly metadata indexes, and found that they are not really suited for non-anglophone monographs and grey literature, which constitutes a significant aspect of our corpus. He proposed an alternative solution: to use Grobid to extract bibliographic references from PDFs using targeted machine learning algorithms.
This approach has a few caveats: We need full and clean PDFs of all works in the corpus, which may be particularly challenging for books. Julie has this covered based on her extensive library and teaching materials. For works that are published as part of anthologies and edited volumes, we also need to isolate references for each chapter or book section. Zack will develop a workflow to assist with this vetting, and Isak will test it out.
This led to some discussion about the nature and scope of the corpus. We reiterated the sense that we should be led by the questions and the practical analytical challenges, rather than the data contained in the seed paper. For instance, the disproportionate number of references in a book relative to a journal article may affect the constitution of a network and generate misleading findings (especially regarding centrality metrics), and it may be prudent to exclude them, or to replace them with a series of papers by the same author that cover the same ground as the book. Moreover, an excavation report may be more descriptive and engage with the literature to a lesser extent than an “standalone” study (for lack of a better term right now), and we may want to discard those. These considerations make the difference between an “easy” bibliometric analysis and a meaningful one.

title: Discussion Topics
text:
Miscellaneous
Zack mentioned his brief social media interactions, which pointed to Christian Bergeron’s recent work with the same/similar toolsets, and whose presentation in April coincidentally helped inspire those whole project. Zack is also consulting with Till Grallert, who develops software to convert between TEI and bibtex (among other data formats used to store bibliographic data). It’s great that we’re relying so much on tools developed by the digital humanities!
We addressed the general plans for the workshop, which we agreed we should hold in March. This will provide greater opportunity to generate meaningful findings and to invite other interesting participants.

title: Discussion
text:
Developing a controlled vocabulary

Three axes:

Topics: What is the paper about? (i.e. diaspora, mobility, gender, ritual, etc)
Methods: What methods were applied in the paper? (i.e. spatial analysis, genetics, stable isotope analysis, finds analysis)
Kind of contribution (i.e. field report, “standard” scientific paper, review of prior work, opinion)

The medium (i.e. journal article, book, chapter in an edited volume, etc) will be identified by CrossRef and does not need to be annotated.
It’s ok to assign multiple terms to each record.

title: Discussion
text:
Coding process

A research assistant will be able to start work in September, and will be able to work for four weeks.
Limited to review of titles and abstracts, or if there is no abstract, the introductions and conclusions.
Since this does not involve comprehensive or open coding, we can just do this in a spreadsheet rather than some specialized QDA software.
The research assistant will ideally be a more experienced student in the field of Viking Age archaeology.
Zack will schedule weekly check-ins with the research assistant and make himself available to address any methodological questions or concerns.

title: Discussion
text:
Analysis of references

We won’t be able to qualitatively annotate references due to lack of time relative to the corpus’ volume.
NLP using scite is not as useful as initially thought.

tends to “play it safe” by coding references as neutral mentions when human coders identify a more robust stance (see Bakker et al. 2023).
Its corpus is limited to works put out by partnered publishers.

Potential alternative to scite, but requires greater knowledge of NLP to implement:

https://github.com/davidjurgens/citation-function
https://jurgens.people.si.umich.edu/citation-function

We may be able to derive a sample based on network statistics, i.e. the most or least central references.

title: Discussion
text:
Analysis of gender

Our intent is to identify citation biases against women.
The goal is not to identify gender diversity, which is not supported by our method.

title: Discussion
text:
Predictions and expectations

We’re gonna find sub-clusters within clusters, and bridging clusters.
Some sub-clusters will be tight-knit and closed, others very broad and open.
Some will be very focused on specific topics.
There will be many links across institutions, they are not really that fixed.
Some citation chains will emerge that reflect casual observations (just a few examples):

Lots of cross-references within the Mälaren valley community.
Tight-knit cluster among papers that are concerned with ritual.
Major computational cluster at Aarhus.

If had a broader time horizon, we might be able to trace “genealogies of affiliation” by tracing how identities change based on the evolution of their collaborative networks.
Clustering in methods by “academic upbringing”, which has a localized character
We may be able to find associations based on age, but mainly by doing a rough assessment of the n most and least central nodes, rather than keying age into the data.

title: Discussion
text:
Additional ideas and insights

Keeping track of topics independently from citational links enables us to validate whether topics are actually clustered around certain individuals or papers, or whether there are diverse centres.
We’ll be able to do some non-network descriptive statistics:

Distribution of topics by affiliations of authors.
Distribution of topics by number of co-authors.
Temporal distributions of genders of lead authors.
Gender of lead author by size and genders of their co-authors.

title: Discussion
text:
Logistics

Keep things on GitHub for now.
Keep our eyes open for alternative collaborative writing platforms that may emerge over the next few months (including via the archaeo-social collective).

title: Codebook
text:
Topics
Coders will mark an X if the record deals with a stated topic. Coders may also reference additional topics in the “Other” field under the Topics category. Overall comments about any record should be made in overall “Comments” field in the Other category.
Trade
Trade, economy, silver, weight looms, dirhems, coins.
This topic covers papers working with economic issues, including the organisation of the trade, the use of balance weights and weight looms, the flow of silver, including dirhems and British, Continental and Scandinavian coins.
Diaspora
Diaspora, migration, mobility.
This topic covers papers dealing with material traces of mobility and migration. Further, paper studying the Viking diaspora as a concept and the material traces of it are included in this topic.
Gender
Gender, Viking women, queer, masculinity.
This topic covers papers on gender and genders, including papers specifically relating to women or men as a category, papers dealing with queer and queer theory, including the discussion of Odinn as queer. Further, discussions of hegemonic masculinity and other aspects of masculinity (and femininity, but I have not seen any papers on the issue) are included in this topic.
Identity
Identity, identities, intersectionality.
This topic covers papers studying various issues of identity, including intersectionality. A number of papers will overlap between this topic and the topics Gender and Diaspora. Further, lifeways and aspects of economy that deal with occupation such as tradespersons and craftspersons may be included in this topic, if the papers explicitly deal with the identity of tradespersons, including tradesmen and tradeswomen and craftsmen and craftswomen.
Violence
Violence, warriors, raids, war, piracy, army.
This topic relates to papers working with traces of plunder, piracy, violence, and warfare. Further, papers on warriors may overlap with the topic identity and gender. Papers working with the material traces of armies, including army camps are also part of this topic. Further, the construction of defence systems, earth works, fortresses and ring fortresses are included in this topic.
Ethnicity
Ethnicity, creolisation, hybridisation, Old Norse and Sámi population.
This topic covers papers relating to discussion of ethnicity as part of social identity studies. Papers examining the material aspects of creolisation and hybridisation are included in this topic as is more essentialistic studies of ethnicity. Papers working with the differences and similarities between Old Norse/Germanic and Sámi populations are part of this topic as is studies of meetings between Inuit and Old Norse populations in Greenland and between Old Norse and Native Americans as well as Inuit populations in Newfoundland. This topic may have overlaps with papers exploring the Viking Diaspora, and with mobility and migration.
Enslaved
Slaves, trell, enslaved, unfree.
This topic covers papers dealing with the social dynamics between free and enslaved. It includes studies of settlements structures with examinations of ‘the room behind the byre’ as well as pit house studies focusing on social differences and unfree and trell (Old Norse for unfree) population members. Further, studies of burials with more than one individual as well as graves with few or no grave goods interpreted as unfree are included. In addition, a number of stabile isotope studies of food and nutrition with discussion of social differences in foods due to unfree social status are included in this topic.
Power
Power, chiefs, magnates, kings, anarchistic perspectives, social organisation, central places and power.
This topic deals with analyses of power relations, manifestations of power and social organisation. Papers relating to magnates and kings and their social position and manifestations of it are included in this topic. Further, analyses building on anarchistic perspectives of power and collective action theory challenging the dominating discourse of power are included in this topic. Further, the analyses of settlement and regions with focus on central places and their position for redistribution of goods in a center-periphery model are included.
World views
Cosmology, world view, ontology, the Viking way, religion, the cognitive landscape, Old Norse and Sámi religion in the Viking Age.
This topic deals with studies of religion, world views, ontology and cosmology. Further, studies of what Neil Price has termed ‘The Viking Way’ as a specific cognitive field or approach are included. Analyses of actions conducted in the landscape as part of creating, maintaining, and dealing with the cognitive or cosmological landscape are part of this topic.
Personhood
Personhood, animated objects, human-non human relationship, post-humanism and the Viking Age.
This topic covers studies of the boundaries between humans and the material world, including human-animal relationship, personhood studies of graves and hoards, and papers working with post-humanistic perspectives as part of their approach to studying the Viking Age. This topic may have overlaps with studies of world views, the Viking Way and Old Norse religion.
Environment
Environment, climate, seasonality, resilience.
This topic covers studies of climate changes and adaption to different climates and seasonal variation in the use of the landscape and its resources. Studies of resilience in relation to the variations during the Late Iron Age are included, if they also covers the Viking Age and not only “the 536/540 AD event”. The topic includes studies of settlements and graves, geoarchaeological studies, and analysis of the use of the landscape in economic terms and its relationship to the condition for farming and other activities in the landscape.
The Viking Ship
Maritime activities, Viking ships.
This topic covers technological analyses of Viking ships, the use of and lack of sail and the symbolic of Viking ships in the Viking Age. The papers included studies finds of Viking ships and the construction and production of them, including tools for ship building. The topic overlaps with studies of migration and mobility as well as with warfare and piracy. Further, this topic may have overlaps with studies of social identity of ship builders based on burial finds.
Includes all work on ships and/or boats, and ship technology, Viking or otherwise (revised December 19).
Rituals
Mortuary practices, burial actions.
This topic covers all studies of ritual actions, including papers studying ritual actions related to the Old Norse and Sámi religion or world view. The performative aspects of burials, their function in society, and the acts of depositions of hoards, tools, and coins may be included in so far as they related to the depositions as rituals.
Memory
Cultural memory, social memory, the use of the past in the Viking Age.
This topic covers all papers studying cultural, social or collective memory. Papers analysing the use and reuse of older structures and antiquities in the Viking Age are included in this topic. The papers may be dealing with the commemorative aspects present in settlements, burial rituals and in hoards. This topic may have overlaps with studies of ritual actions and world views.
Craft
Craft, production, spinning, weaving, non-ferrous metal, smithing, comb making, ceramics.
This topic covers papers working with craft and production at urban as well as rural settings. Production sites as well as traces of craft and production on the individual objects are included in this topic. This topic may have overlap with outfield resources.
Outfield resources
Living in the outfield, extraction of resources in the outfields, iron production, tar production, soap stone vessel production.
This topic covers outfield economy and lifeway and the extraction of resources in the outfield areas. This topic may have overlaps with craft and hunting as well as with studies of ethnicity and intersectionality.
Hunting
Hunting, hunting pits, hunting pit systems, scaring sticks, arrows, snow patch finds.
This topic covers papers dealing with hunting activities. Snow patch finds of scaring sticks and bone and iron arrow heads and arrows are also included in this topic. This topic may have overlaps with studies of ethnicity.
Other
Additional topics identified by the coder.
Heritage
Contemporary views of the past. To be more closely examined as a focus of investigation later.

title: Codebook
text:
Methodology

Sources of Evidence
The material basis upon which a study depends.
Graves and monuments
Contexts of memorialized human remains, including artefacts, monuments, and the remains themselves.
Revised (December 19) to include monuments, including rune stones.
Hoards
A collection of valuable objects or artifacts, sometimes purposely buried in the ground.
Settlements
Places of human habitation.
Emporia
Trading settlements characterized by their peripheral locations, their lack of infrastructure and their short-lived nature.
Other structures, sites of production or pit systems
May include quarries, smithies, mines or middens.
Portable artefacts
Human-made objects that are not fixed in place.
Human biological remains
Human bones, teeth or soft tissue preserved in the archaeological record.
Non-anthropogenic materials
Animal or plant remains, geological specimens, features of the natural landscape.
Stray finds
Metal-detector finds, items from historic museum archives, or other finds that lack complete contextual information.
Written sources
Poetry, inscriptions, sagas, annals, and other sources from the Viking Age and Mediaval Era.
Ethnographic sources
Observations of cultural practice, social organizations, or Indigenous lifeways, and scholarly interpretations thereof.


Methods
The mode of analysis through which materials are examined to derive additional knowledge.
aDNA
Analysis of DNA from archaeological or anthropological sources, including skeletons of humans, domesticate animal or plants, artefacts, or cave sediments.
Biological analyses
Osteoarchaeology, analysis of preserved soft tissue.
Concerned with the biological study of bones, teeth and other human biological remains available in the archaeological record.
Palaeoenvironment reconstruction
Zooarchaeology, archaeobotany, pollen and phytolith analysis.
Concerned with better understanding past environments in which humans lived through analysis of non-human biological remains.
Stable isotope analyses
Analysis of Strontium, Oxygen and Nitrogen in teeth and bone.
Identification of the relatively abundance of isotopic elements in organic and inorganic compounds, to reconstruct ancient food webs or to reconstruct past environmental and climatic conditions.
Absolute dating
Radiocarbon dating, dendrochronology, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL).
Determination of absolute dates through scientific means. May involve analysis of stable isotopes (C14, Potassium-Argon, Uranium-Lead), measuring doses of ionizing radiation (OSL), or by counting characteristic patterns of annual change in the natural environment (dendrochronology).
Geophysical analyses
Geoarchaeology, ground penetrating radar, LiDAR.
Application of geology and earth science methods. May also include systematic collection and analysis of geophysical signals, such as magnetic and gravitational fields emanating from the earth.
Geochemical analyses
X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF), Instrumental Neutron activation analysis, Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS).
Techniques for identifying the elemental composition of physical objects.
Spatial analysis
Regional distributions, viewshed analysis, distributions in relationship to landscape features, GIS.
Identification and analysis of patterns relating to spatial distributions or relationships.
Artefact analysis
Analysis of pottery, lithics and other portable objects preserved in the archaeological record. Includes 3D scanning and analysis of artefacts.
Identification and comparison of artefacts’ physical features. May also include advanced computer-assisted shape-recognition techniques to automatically classify objects based on input representations of their physical shapes or morphological properties.
Literary analysis and epigraphy
Analysis of myths, sagas, runes and inscriptions.
Techniques for examining ancient texts and symbols.
Quantitative or statistical analysis
Multivariate analysis, similarity measurements, multidimensional scaling, principal components analysis, cluster analysis, network analysis, agent-based modelling and simulation.
Identification and analysis of quantitative distributions of object types and features.
Discourse analysis
Analysis and reflection regarding the ideas and attitudes expressed by the community of practice that investigates the Viking Age.
Relative Dating
Typological comparison and other means of relative dating (to be identified as we go).

title: Part 3 — Joining structural and annotation descriptions
text:
Everything in Part 1 describes the annotation data on its own terms; everything in Part 2 describes the graph on its own terms. Neither is a baseline the other is checked against. This section places them side by side and reads the relationship, which is where the actual analytical content of this project lives.

community_gn (Girvan-Newman, fragmentation-onset cut) is checked here against the topics, methods, and sources of evidence coded in Part 1, for both versions of the graph. Annotated uses the cut of the Annotated run and Annotated, seed filtered uses the cut of the seed-filtered run. The comparison is restricted to works with a matching annotation (F1-only; see the join above), which is 369 works in Annotated and 369 in Annotated, seed filtered. Louvain and Leiden cluster assignments also exist from Part 2 but are not used in this section.
Coverage is thin relative to the graph as a whole: in Annotated, 369 annotated works out of 12697 nodes, and within any single cluster that annotated count is often a small fraction of the cluster’s real size (the heatmaps below show the clusters tied for the 20 most annotated works, 33 in Annotated and 47 in Annotated, seed filtered, and no cluster holds more than 4 annotated works out of a much larger true membership). A prior exploratory pass on an earlier GN cut of this same corpus found 7-13 annotated nodes per cluster typical, out of hundreds of members, and treated agreement between structure and annotation as directionally suggestive rather than comprehensively verified for that reason. The same caution applies here: what follows can show that structure and coding line up somewhere, but cannot rule out that the uncoded majority of any cluster tells a different story.
The coded columns are wide, one column per topic/method/source category, valued "Primary", "Secondary", or blank. Primary and secondary are merged throughout what follows: a work counts as coded with a category at either level, matching the method used in a prior exploratory pass on an earlier GN cut of this corpus. A work can carry more than one topic, method, or source, so per-cluster percentages below do not sum to 100%; each cell shows the raw count behind its percentage for transparency.
How to read the enrichment heatmaps below. Raw coverage (what fraction of a cluster’s annotated works carry a given category) is misleading on its own: some categories are common across the whole corpus regardless of cluster — “Spatial analysis” as a method, or “Environment” as a topic, show up in most clusters simply because most works in this corpus use them, not because any one cluster is distinctively characterized by them. To separate genuine distinctiveness from corpus-wide popularity, each heatmap cell instead shows enrichment: a cluster’s coverage of a category divided by that category’s rate across the whole annotated corpus. A value of 1x means the cluster carries the category at exactly the corpus average; 2x means twice the corpus rate; 0.5x means half. White is 1x (baseline); blue is above baseline (the category is over-represented in that cluster, a real distinguishing signal); red is below baseline (under-represented). For example, if “Palaeoenvironment reconstruction” is coded in 23% of the whole corpus but 100% of a given cluster’s annotated works, that cell shows roughly 4.4x — a real signal that environmental method is disproportionately concentrated there, not just present because it’s common everywhere.


Girvan-Newman clusters by topic. A threshold of 3+ annotated works lets through only a small share of the clusters in this corpus (see the counts below), so it does not give a workable set. Shown here instead, in the heatmap below: the clusters tied for the 20 most annotated works (33 in Annotated and 47 in Annotated, seed filtered, because many clusters tie at two annotated works). This is a readability choice, not a derived breakpoint.
At this cut, Annotated has 794 clusters, 5 of which pass a 3+ annotated-works threshold, and its largest cluster is 30 members larger than the second-largest. Annotated, seed filtered has 595 clusters, 5 of which pass the threshold, and its largest cluster is 17 members larger than the second-largest.
Coverage varies a lot by cluster (annotation is thin relative to true cluster size, per the caveat above), so each row label shows how many annotated works its percentages are based on, out of the cluster’s true total size.

The topic, method, and source enrichment findings above surface individual standout cells one at a time. title: Part 1 — Annotation descriptives
text:
Gender
Author gender, examined two ways: first-author gender and all-author gender by year, and gender composition across the full author list per paper.

By year





Top: first author only, one bar per gender per year — faint bars mean few papers published that year. Bottom: every author position pooled (order not preserved), so a multi-author paper contributes more than one tally — faint bars there mean few author-slots that year, not few papers. Same Wilson-interval fade used throughout this document, computed against the relevant denominator for each panel.






Composition across the full author list
First-author gender and the order-blind pool above don’t capture gender composition per paper (all-male vs. all-female vs. mixed) or order within a paper.









Several ways of collapsing a per-paper gender sequence into a single cross-tabbable category are compared below — a strict all-same-vs-mixed split, a majority-based split, and a version that separates solo authorship out from multi-author teams (since “all-male” means something different for n=1 than for a genuinely uniform team).

title: Part 1 — Annotation descriptives
text:
Topic
A paper can carry a Primary-coded topic (the coder’s judgment of its main focus) and any number of Secondary-coded topics (also present, but not the main focus) — see the codebook for the exact scope of each topic category. title: Part 1 — Annotation descriptives
text:
Region










Matching to Wikidata
Region is free text drawn directly from each paper, not a controlled vocabulary: spelling variants and mixed specificity (continent, country, named site) count as distinct terms in the word cloud above. Wikidata is used to consolidate these to real places with coordinates. Pleiades, Pelagios/Peripleo, and iDAI.gazetteer were considered and set aside: all three are institutionally anchored in Mediterranean/classical-world antiquity, with no confirmed non-trivial coverage of Viking-Age Scandinavia. Wikidata was used instead for its dense, well-curated coverage of Scandinavian archaeological sites and structured multilingual labels/aliases, which handle spelling variants (Danmark/Denmark) close to for free.
The chunks below call Wikidata’s SPARQL endpoint and so require outbound network access; they default to eval: false and do not run on a normal render of this document. Run them explicitly (flip eval: true) when the lookup table needs building or refreshing, then leave them off again — the rest of this section reads the resulting static CSV, same as Topic, Method, and Source read their own derived data.
Coverage probe. Before matching all tokens, check hit rate on the most frequent ones — this is the actual empirical check for whether Wikidata is workable here, not an assumption.
Check probe_results before continuing. If the hit rate on real, frequent Viking-Age placenames (Birka, Hedeby, Kaupang, Ribe, Uppåkra, Tissø, etc.) is low, the class filter above may be too narrow — Wikidata items for archaeological sites are not always tagged with exactly these instance of values — and the SPARQL query needs revising before running the full match. A high count under contains fallback is expected and fine — it means the class filter is right but the corpus token is a shortened form of the item’s real label (e.g. “Gokstad” for “Gokstad Mound”), not a coverage problem.
Full match, once the probe above confirms acceptable coverage. This single chunk matches every token, separates out macro-region terms that can’t resolve to a point, and writes the resulting lookup table plus a manual-review export, all together (previously three separate chunks; merged into one so a single eval flag controls the whole matching-to- saved-file pipeline, since matching without saving the result was wasted work run for nothing):
Nesting (optional). Every matched place is currently flat: “Birka,” “Vestfold,” “Sweden,” and “Scandinavia” are independent tokens with no recorded relationship between them, even though Birka is genuinely in Uppland, Sweden, Scandinavia. This chunk resolves three nesting levels for each matched place, each as its own column:

admin_region — the first P131 (“located in the administrative territorial entity”) ancestor above the site itself, before reaching the country: a county, province, or similar (e.g. Birka → Uppland). Not every place has a clean single admin-region ancestor in Wikidata; those are left NA rather than guessed.
country — walked further up P131* to the first ancestor that is itself a country (Wikidata class Q6256).
super_region — not derived from Wikidata at all. Unlike country, there is no single reliable Wikidata class for “super-region” in the sense this corpus uses the term (Scandinavia, British Isles, Baltic states); these are real, well-understood historical/cultural groupings, not administrative ones, so this is a small, explicit, hand-authored country → super-region mapping instead of an automatically-derived one. Extend super_region_map below as more countries appear in the resolved data.

Like the matching chunks above, this calls Wikidata and needs network access; it stays off by default.
Country resolution here runs on the raw matched coordinates, before the known_bad_matches correction is applied (that correction lives in region-joined below, and only nulls the bad matches’ lat/lon/etc. there, not here). So resolving nesting right after this chunk can produce a real country value for a token later corrected to no_match — e.g. “Repton” resolving to “United States” here, even though region-joined clears it entirely downstream. That correction was extended to also null admin_region/country/super_region when present, so this is handled automatically as long as region-joined runs after nesting, which it always does on a normal render.
Once region_lookup.csv exists, the resulting region_df joins region to gender, topic, method, source, and year the same way those variables already join to each other elsewhere in this document — by citekey, using the same Wilson-interval and by-year machinery.


Where the corpus is set
Most of the real signal in Region is simply where papers are concentrated geographically — a stacked gender-composition bar chart like the ones used for Topic, Method, and Source needs several well-populated categories to say anything real, and Region has one (Birka, 20 papers) with a steep drop to a long tail of 1-3-paper tokens, so that chart type doesn’t suit this variable the way it suits the others. Two more direct views instead: where the named, point-matched places actually are, and how concentrated the corpus really is by raw count.
What the map includes. A region token appears as a point only if it has a real matched coordinate, is not a macro-region term (Scandinavia, Viking world, East Baltic, and the rest of that list — excluded even when Wikidata does return a coordinate for the concept, since a single point can’t honestly represent an area that broad), and falls within a fixed plotting bounding box (lat 25-80, lon -60 to 100) that excludes a couple of real but geographically irrelevant matches (Oceania, Pacific Ocean) which would otherwise force the whole map out to a global scale. Dot size is the number of papers carrying that exact region token — 20 papers all tagged “Birka” produce one dot sized 20, not 20 separate dots. The map’s crop is computed from the real spread of whatever points pass all three filters, with a fixed margin, so it always fits what’s actually shown rather than a hardcoded guess.





Named places mentioned in the corpus, sized by number of papers. Macro-region terms (Scandinavia, Viking world, and similar) are excluded even when Wikidata returns a coordinate for them, since a single point cannot honestly represent an area that broad — see the totals chart below for those. Cropped to the real spread of the remaining matched coordinates with a margin; a handful of correct but far-flung matches (e.g. Oceania, Pacific Ocean — real tokens in the corpus, real Wikidata matches) fall outside this crop and are not shown on the map.









Every region token with at least 3 tagged papers, point-matched places and macro-region terms together, ranked by raw count.




By country (optional, requires country nesting). The chart above keeps every region token flat, “Birka” and “Sweden” and “Scandinavia” are three separate bars even though Birka is in Sweden — deliberately, since the paper’s own choice of a site-level or country-level term is itself part of what the data says, not noise to collapse away. This alternate view rolls site-level tags up to the country they’re actually in, using the country column added by the region-nesting chunk above (only present once that chunk has been run). A paper tagged “Birka” counts toward Sweden here even if it was never separately tagged “Sweden.” Macro-region terms (Scandinavia, Viking world) still have no single country and are excluded from this view.





Papers per country, site-level tags rolled up to their containing country.






Topic, method, and source by region
Same problem as gender composition above: most region tokens have too few papers to support a per-region proportion chart. Enrichment solves this differently — restricted to regions with at least 5 tagged papers, each cell shows that region’s coverage of a topic/method/source divided by that category’s own rate across the whole corpus (1.0x = corpus average), the same measure already used for cluster structure in Part 3. A region’s low paper count still means less certainty behind its cells, but enrichment at least says something real about direction even on a modest sample, where a stacked-proportion chart on the same sample would mostly just show noise. All three heatmaps below share the same region row order, so a region’s profile can be compared directly across tabs.

TopicMethodSource of evidence







Topic enrichment by region (regions with 5+ tagged papers only). White = topic at corpus average rate for that region; blue = above average; red = below. Cell shows raw count behind the percentage. Capped at 3x so a handful of extreme small-n ratios don’t wash out the rest of the scale.











Method enrichment by region (regions with 5+ tagged papers only). Same reading as the topic heatmap above.











Source-of-evidence enrichment by region (regions with 5+ tagged papers only). Same reading as the topic heatmap above.









Topic, method, and source by administrative level
The tabset above groups by the raw region token as written in each paper, “Birka” and “Sweden” stay separate rows even though one is inside the other. This section repeats the same topic/method/source enrichment analysis, but grouped at each of the three nesting levels resolved by the region-nesting chunk above instead: admin region, country, and super-region. Requires that chunk to have been run at least once — each tab below checks for its column and explains what to do if it’s missing.
The enrichment baseline here is different from the tabset above, on purpose: each cell compares a group’s rate against the rate among only the papers that resolved to some value at that nesting level, not against the whole 369-paper F1 corpus. The flat-token tabset above uses the whole-corpus rate, since every F1 paper is a fair comparison point for a raw region tag. Nesting-level resolution is a narrower subset (only papers whose region successfully resolved up to a country, say), so comparing against the whole corpus would dilute the baseline with papers that never entered this analysis at all and understate real enrichment within the resolved set. Enrichment numbers are therefore not directly comparable between the two tabsets, even when they group the same underlying papers.

By admin regionBy countryBy super-region




























































































Change over time
Does the corpus’s geographic focus shift across the years covered, more Iceland/Greenland work recently versus more mainland Scandinavia earlier, or the reverse? Same problem as the other region breakdowns: most tokens have too few papers spread across too many years to support a real per-year trend. Restricted to regions with at least 8 tagged papers (a higher bar than the 5-paper threshold used for the topic/method/source heatmaps above, since splitting an already-small group by year further thins each cell), using the same Wilson-interval and enrichment machinery already defined for Topic, Method, and Source.





Papers per year, per region (regions with 8+ tagged papers only). Faint bars: few papers that year.









Enrichment per year, per region (regions with 8+ tagged papers only) — that year’s coverage of the region, divided by the region’s own average coverage across the whole corpus (1.0x, dashed line = normal). Faint bars: few papers that year.

title: Part 0: Corpus overview
text:
From seed paper to corpus
The F1 corpus is built from the bibliography of the seed paper (Lund & Sindbæk 2022): its cited references, treated as a first generation of descendant works. The seed paper’s own reference list resolves to 576 works in the bibliography; the F1 corpus analyzed here holds 369, meaning 207 references were excluded.

Selection criteria
Two exclusion criteria were applied when building the F1 set from the seed paper’s reference list:

Full books and edited volumes with consolidated bibliographies. A book’s reference list is not comparable in scale or character to a journal article’s, and including it as a single node alongside articles would distort network measures, centrality in particular, that depend on reference-list size.
Methodological/technical reports outside the study’s interpretive scope, judged case by case. One paper (Cannell et al. 2016, a geochemical pXRF methods chapter in an edited excavation volume) was excluded on this basis; it remains in the wider bibliography as a citation target for the papers that cite it, but was removed from the annotated F1 seed set.

No other structured record of exclusion reasons for the remaining works in the seed’s reference list currently exists; this count has not yet been individually itemized and categorized beyond these two documented criteria.

title: Part 0: Corpus overview
text:
Citation detection per F1 paper





Distribution of outgoing (resolved) citation counts across the F1 corpus.




Every F1 paper has at least one resolved outgoing citation, and the citation graph as a whole forms a single connected component. This was not the case throughout corpus construction: extraction passes repeatedly left individual F1 papers disconnected, most often from a reference-list format (footnote-embedded citations, a shared reference section for an edited volume, non-Latin or corrupted encoding) the primary extraction method did not handle, or from the same work being independently extracted twice under two citekeys. Each case was resolved against the original source PDF or documented as a genuine structural exception.

title: Part 0: Corpus overview
text:
From detection to resolved bibliography
The citation graph is built in two stages: automated detection of candidate citations per paper, then manual correction and deduplication across the whole bibliography.



Raw citation detections by method, before merging duplicate detections of the same citation


Detection method
Raw detections




Structured reference list (GROBID)
24560


Inline citation markers

Each paper’s PDF is scanned by six independent methods: GROBID parsing its structured reference list, matching inline citation markers in the body text, text-pattern matching, and three LLM-based passes (a body-text scan, a bibliography reparse, and a footnote scan). A single real citation is frequently flagged by more than one method. The 66,683 raw detections above merge down to 31,994 deduplicated citations per-paper, which are then carried into the bibliography-wide correction process below. The structured reference list and inline-marker matching account for the large majority of raw detections; the LLM-based methods contribute the remainder, recovering citations the structured parser misses, most commonly footnote-embedded references and citations in non-standard or non-Latin formats. 1.16% of bibliography entries (167) have no title recorded: a paper in the corpus cites them, but the entry itself has no title or an incomplete author.
Once detected, citations are carried into a single shared bibliography, where the same underlying work can be independently detected from multiple citing papers and needs consolidating into one record. This consolidation, along with other manual corrections, is tracked in a running corrections file (corrections.yaml) rather than as edits to the raw pipeline output.



Manual, individually-reasoned correction actions applied to the bibliography (corrections.yaml)






Action
Count

17528

Two bulk, mechanical field backfills are tracked in the same file but excluded from the table above: a language value was set on 12,807 entries and a detection value on 12,804 entries, both copied wholesale from the pipeline’s own processing cache rather than individually reasoned. Combined they account for more set actions than every other correction in the file put together, so are reported separately to avoid making the file’s manual-correction volume look larger than it is.
As of this writing the file holds 20753 individually-reasoned correction actions, plus the 25,611 bulk field backfills noted above. The great majority of delete actions removed “ghost” entries: records with no title and no raw citation text, produced when the extraction pipeline generated a placeholder entry it was never able to resolve to a real source. merge actions consolidated cases where the same underlying work had been independently created under two or more citekeys, most commonly because one version came from an automated reference-list extraction with no linked PDF and a second, fuller version was later created when the paper’s own PDF was located and processed directly, or because the same source was independently extracted from two different citing papers’ reference lists, the cross-paper duplication this section exists to resolve. set actions in the table above cover routine field-level corrections: fixing fabricated or garbled author names, correcting mis-parsed years and titles, and adding real citation relationships (cited_by entries) that automated detection missed or failed to resolve on the first pass.
One deletion in this file was subsequently confirmed incorrect and reversed: a genuine F1 paper had been marked fabricated across multiple earlier review passes despite being a real, verifiable source, and was restored with corrected metadata once checked directly against its source PDF. This is noted here as a reminder that delete corrections, like any other, should be treated as provisional until checked against a primary source rather than as settled fact on the strength of a confident-sounding note.

In-degree (times cited within the corpus) and out-degree (number of works cited) capture different roles. High in-degree identifies widely-cited works — the intellectual anchors of the field. High out-degree identifies works that are heavily engaged with the literature, drawing on many sources.
Betweenness centrality identifies works that sit on many shortest paths between other works — brokers between sub-literatures. Betweenness is expensive to compute on large graphs; both normalized and raw values are reported. Normalized divides by the theoretical maximum for a graph this size (roughly (n-1)(n-2) for a directed graph), so on a graph with over 12,697 nodes even a genuinely high-betweenness work normalizes to a very small fraction — small in absolute terms, not because the work is unimportant. Raw values, not rescaled, are more intuitively legible for comparing works directly against each other.
PageRank assigns authority based on incoming links weighted by the authority of the linking node — conceptually similar to being cited by works that are themselves widely cited. Hub and authority scores (HITS) are complementary: hubs point to many authorities; authorities are pointed to by many hubs.
Peripheral works — low degree, low centrality by every measure below — are not treated as noise in this project. A work cited only once may be exactly the interesting case (a niche, contested, or newly emerging reference) for a study of citational politics. No node is excluded from any measure in this section on the basis of low degree.

A negative relationship between publication year and betweenness is expected as a baseline structural effect, independent of any specific work’s importance: an older work has had more time to accumulate citations from both earlier and later literature, giving it more opportunities to sit on shortest paths between clusters that didn’t yet exist when it was published. The interesting question is not whether that baseline trend exists, but what departs from it: works that are old without being especially well-connected, and, more notably, works that are young but already bridging despite limited time to accumulate citations — those are candidates for genuinely novel synthesis, not just structurally advantaged age.
The trend line4 in the first plot of each tab is fit to the nonzero subset, where the actual bridging signal is. In Annotated, 0 of the 367 works with nonzero betweenness (0%) were published before 2000. In Annotated, seed filtered, the figures are 0 of 230 (0%). The second plot in each tab shows every work, including the zero-betweenness majority, so the shape of any boundary between old and recent works is visible directly.

Older works therefore score zero whatever their place in the literature, and these plots cannot compare old and recent works. The k-core of a graph is the maximal subgraph in which every node has at least k connections to other nodes within that subgraph. It is computed by iteratively removing nodes with degree below k until no further removal is possible. A node’s coreness is the highest k for which it still belongs to the k-core: a coreness of 1 means the node only survives the weakest possible core (removed as soon as k reaches 2), while a high coreness means the node stays embedded even as the graph is stripped down to only its most densely-interconnected parts.
K-core decomposition is reported here purely as a descriptive measure, showing which works sit in dense mutual-citation relationships versus which sit at the periphery, following Alvarez-Hamelin et al. (2005). Every work, regardless of its coreness, is still included in full in every other analysis in this document: coreness only describes a work’s position, it doesn’t filter anything out.
Coreness and in-degree measure genuinely different things, worth comparing directly: in-degree simply counts how many times a work is cited, with no regard for whether those citing works are themselves well-connected. Coreness asks a structurally deeper question, whether a work sits inside a neighborhood that is itself densely interconnected, not just cited often in isolation. A work could have high in-degree while sitting at low coreness, if most of its citations come from otherwise peripheral, poorly-connected works; conversely, a work with only moderate in-degree can have high coreness if it’s embedded in a tightly interlinked core. The tables below show whether these two measures broadly agree on this corpus, or diverge in informative ways.

At the highest coreness (k = 8), Annotated holds 287 works. 5 of them are also among the five most cited and 5 among the five highest-betweenness works. In Annotated, seed filtered, the highest coreness is k = 7 with 381 works, of which 5 are among the five most cited and 5 among the five highest-betweenness works. Where in-degree, betweenness and k-core point to the same few works, that is a stronger, cross-validated signal than any one measure alone: those works are central by several different, genuinely distinct criteria at once.



Community detection here produces several independent descriptions of how the graph divides, not a single answer to be triangulated. Louvain (Blondel et al. 2008) and Leiden (Traag, Waltman, and Eck 2019) ask “which groups of nodes are more densely interconnected than a random graph with the same degree sequence would predict,” a notion formalized as modularity (M. E. J. Newman 2006). Girvan-Newman (Girvan and Newman 2002) asks “which edges, if removed, disconnect otherwise-separate parts of the network.” K-means asks a third, differently-grounded question again: not about graph structure at all, but about each work’s centrality profile, grouping works that occupy similar structural positions, for example highly-cited authorities vs. high-betweenness brokers vs. peripheral works.








Note



Louvain, Leiden and K-means are computed for both graphs in graph_metrics() with no visible output. Their agreement across the two graphs is reported in “What the seed filter changes”. The plotting code for each is kept in the appendix, disabled; toggle eval: true on any of those chunks to render it.







Louvain and Leiden each partition the graph once, at one resolution, and return a single result. Girvan-Newman (Girvan and Newman 2002) instead removes edges one at a time: at each step, it identifies the edge with the highest betweenness centrality (the edge carrying the largest number of shortest paths between all pairs of nodes in the graph), removes it, and recomputes betweenness for the remaining edges before repeating. Because a shortest path between two densely connected regions of a graph usually has to cross whichever single edge joins them, that edge tends to have disproportionately high betweenness and is removed early, while edges internal to a well-connected region, which have many alternative paths around them, are removed only much later. The result is a record of the entire removal sequence, from the original, fully connected graph down to every paper standing alone: a dendrogram. The tree below is that record. Height represents the order in which components split apart, not the raw round number, since the actual rounds are spaced too unevenly to remain legible on a linear axis; left-right position carries no information and is arranged only to avoid crossing branches.

AnnotatedAnnotated, seed filtered




























Girvan-Newman, in its original form, does not select a stopping point from this sequence (Fortunato 2010); the removal process continues until no edges remain. A refinement published two years after the original algorithm (M. E. Newman and Girvan 2004) selects the round with the highest modularity score as the working partition, and this is the conventional choice, but it fails on this corpus: modularity continues to rise as the graph fragments, reaching its maximum only once 94.2% of nodes are singleton communities (94.3% of nodes in the seed filtered run), which is not a usable partition. This is a documented limitation of modularity on sparse networks, where it can lack a clear maximum and instead admit many different high-scoring partitions (Good, de Montjoye, and Clauset 2010). The criterion used instead counts connected components directly: the point where that count starts climbing steadily, one round after another, marks where the graph is actually breaking into pieces, independent of whether modularity happens to be rising or falling at the same time. The earliest such round is 9,312 (Annotated) and 8,700 (Annotated, seed filtered), and it is used for every community grouping in the rest of this document.

The graph above shows how many citations pass between clusters, and that count depends heavily on how large each cluster is. This test asks whether the citations from one cluster land in another cluster more or less often than chance would put them there, for the 20 clusters in the graph. This section identifies each cluster’s most-cited papers by within-cluster citation degree, then has a language model write a label and description from their titles, independent of the F1 annotation codebook. Comparing these labels against the codebook happens separately, in 03_joined_descriptions.qmd.
For each cluster, select_representatives.py ranks the cluster’s own papers by how many other members of that cluster cite them, and takes the top few as a representative sample. label_clusters.py sends those titles to a language model, which sorts them into named groups and writes a label and description from the largest group; a second label is written only when a real second group exists with enough titles behind it. Full detail on both steps, including the hub-independence rule and the mechanical checks run on the model’s output, is in cluster_labelling/README.md.

The clusters can be grouped in turn. Two clusters are linked when papers in one cite papers in the other, and also when their citing papers cite many of the same works. A single run of one community-detection method is a weak basis for groups here, because the result changes with the method, the resolution and the definition of a link. The grouping below therefore runs 8 variants, with 5 random seeds each, on every cluster of every size. The variants are Leiden at four resolutions, Louvain, Infomap on undirected and on directed links, and Leiden on shared references. Two clusters share a group when they were grouped together in at least 50% of the runs on average. A cluster forms a group alone when no other cluster meets that test with it, which means the variants disagree about which cluster it belongs with. Each group reports the share of runs in which its members stayed together. A high share is necessary but not enough, because weakly linked clusters can be grouped together consistently without sharing a theme, so the cluster labels in each row need reading as well.

The partition plots above use the Fruchterman-Reingold layout (fr, 500 iterations, with igraph’s grid speed-up). The layouts below were tried and are kept for reference with eval: false. Each calls the same plotting function as the main plots, so any of them can be switched on one at a time and run on either graph.

fr spreads the papers that cite a hub around it, so each community reads as a region of the plot. It runs in seconds on either graph.
lgl with coolexp lowered to 0.5, the layout used before, stretches the graph into one diagonal band and leaves the highlighted communities overlapping through its middle. It is also far slower than fr on the seed-filtered graph.
drl stacks the papers that cite a hub on top of it, so every community collapses into a single dot and the plot shows nothing of its shape.
stress (graphlayouts::layout_with_stress()) is faster than drl and built to preserve graph distance. It produced a concentric-ring pattern and was rejected.
Untuned lgl places a handful of true outliers far from the rest. That is why the main plots crop the view to the 1st to 99th percentile.
lgl with repulserad doubled spread the periphery out and left the inner core dense. repulserad sets the distance at which repulsion stops acting and does not change its strength, so it is the wrong lever for core density.

The Louvain, Leiden and K-means plots, also disabled. Each saves a PNG and a PDF next to this document.



analysis/bibvik_node_table.csv, which 03_joined_descriptions.qmd reads, holds the Annotated graph’s measures with one row per node, plus community_gn from the Annotated run’s earliest cut and community_gn_seed_filtered from the seed-filtered run. group_gn and group_gn_seed_filtered hold the consensus group of each paper’s cluster. The Girvan-Newman columns are left out when a run has not been installed.

title: Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions
text:
In-degree (times cited within the corpus) and out-degree (number of works cited) capture different roles. High in-degree identifies widely-cited works — the intellectual anchors of the field. High out-degree identifies works that are heavily engaged with the literature, drawing on many sources.
Betweenness centrality identifies works that sit on many shortest paths between other works — brokers between sub-literatures. Betweenness is expensive to compute on large graphs; both normalized and raw values are reported. Normalized divides by the theoretical maximum for a graph this size (roughly (n-1)(n-2) for a directed graph), so on a graph with over 12,697 nodes even a genuinely high-betweenness work normalizes to a very small fraction — small in absolute terms, not because the work is unimportant. Raw values, not rescaled, are more intuitively legible for comparing works directly against each other.
PageRank assigns authority based on incoming links weighted by the authority of the linking node — conceptually similar to being cited by works that are themselves widely cited. Hub and authority scores (HITS) are complementary: hubs point to many authorities; authorities are pointed to by many hubs.
Peripheral works — low degree, low centrality by every measure below — are not treated as noise in this project. A work cited only once may be exactly the interesting case (a niche, contested, or newly emerging reference) for a study of citational politics. No node is excluded from any measure in this section on the basis of low degree.

A power-law or scale-free degree distribution is characteristic of citation networks: most works are cited rarely, a small number are cited frequently, visible as a roughly straight-line decline on a log-log plot. The plot below tests whether this corpus follows that pattern.

AnnotatedAnnotated, seed filtered

























The bulk of the distribution follows a fairly straight decline on this log-log scale, consistent with the expected power-law pattern: most works are cited once or twice (86% of works with at least one citation in Annotated and 86% in Annotated, seed filtered), a much smaller number several times. In Annotated, 99% of works with at least one citation are cited eight times or fewer, and 99% in Annotated, seed filtered. The tail is real, not an artifact of a truncated plot axis: the maximum in-degree is 66 in Annotated and 66 in Annotated, seed filtered. A handful of works drive that high-citation tail, listed below rather than relied on to show clearly as bars on the histogram above, since bars this sparse are easy to miss regardless of binning.

A negative relationship between publication year and betweenness is expected as a baseline structural effect, independent of any specific work’s importance: an older work has had more time to accumulate citations from both earlier and later literature, giving it more opportunities to sit on shortest paths between clusters that didn’t yet exist when it was published. The interesting question is not whether that baseline trend exists, but what departs from it: works that are old without being especially well-connected, and, more notably, works that are young but already bridging despite limited time to accumulate citations — those are candidates for genuinely novel synthesis, not just structurally advantaged age.
The trend line4 in the first plot of each tab is fit to the nonzero subset, where the actual bridging signal is. In Annotated, 0 of the 367 works with nonzero betweenness (0%) were published before 2000. In Annotated, seed filtered, the figures are 0 of 230 (0%). The second plot in each tab shows every work, including the zero-betweenness majority, so the shape of any boundary between old and recent works is visible directly.

title: Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions
text:
The k-core of a graph is the maximal subgraph in which every node has at least k connections to other nodes within that subgraph. It is computed by iteratively removing nodes with degree below k until no further removal is possible. A node’s coreness is the highest k for which it still belongs to the k-core: a coreness of 1 means the node only survives the weakest possible core (removed as soon as k reaches 2), while a high coreness means the node stays embedded even as the graph is stripped down to only its most densely-interconnected parts.
K-core decomposition is reported here purely as a descriptive measure, showing which works sit in dense mutual-citation relationships versus which sit at the periphery, following Alvarez-Hamelin et al. (2005). Every work, regardless of its coreness, is still included in full in every other analysis in this document: coreness only describes a work’s position, it doesn’t filter anything out.
Coreness and in-degree measure genuinely different things, worth comparing directly: in-degree simply counts how many times a work is cited, with no regard for whether those citing works are themselves well-connected. Coreness asks a structurally deeper question, whether a work sits inside a neighborhood that is itself densely interconnected, not just cited often in isolation. A work could have high in-degree while sitting at low coreness, if most of its citations come from otherwise peripheral, poorly-connected works; conversely, a work with only moderate in-degree can have high coreness if it’s embedded in a tightly interlinked core. The tables below show whether these two measures broadly agree on this corpus, or diverge in informative ways.

title: Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions
text:
Community detection here produces several independent descriptions of how the graph divides, not a single answer to be triangulated. Louvain (Blondel et al. 2008) and Leiden (Traag, Waltman, and Eck 2019) ask “which groups of nodes are more densely interconnected than a random graph with the same degree sequence would predict,” a notion formalized as modularity (M. E. J. Newman 2006). Girvan-Newman (Girvan and Newman 2002) asks “which edges, if removed, disconnect otherwise-separate parts of the network.” K-means asks a third, differently-grounded question again: not about graph structure at all, but about each work’s centrality profile, grouping works that occupy similar structural positions, for example highly-cited authorities vs. high-betweenness brokers vs. peripheral works.








Note



Louvain, Leiden and K-means are computed for both graphs in graph_metrics() with no visible output. Their agreement across the two graphs is reported in “What the seed filter changes”. The plotting code for each is kept in the appendix, disabled; toggle eval: true on any of those chunks to render it.







Louvain and Leiden each partition the graph once, at one resolution, and return a single result. Girvan-Newman (Girvan and Newman 2002) instead removes edges one at a time: at each step, it identifies the edge with the highest betweenness centrality (the edge carrying the largest number of shortest paths between all pairs of nodes in the graph), removes it, and recomputes betweenness for the remaining edges before repeating. Because a shortest path between two densely connected regions of a graph usually has to cross whichever single edge joins them, that edge tends to have disproportionately high betweenness and is removed early, while edges internal to a well-connected region, which have many alternative paths around them, are removed only much later. The result is a record of the entire removal sequence, from the original, fully connected graph down to every paper standing alone: a dendrogram. The tree below is that record. Height represents the order in which components split apart, not the raw round number, since the actual rounds are spaced too unevenly to remain legible on a linear axis; left-right position carries no information and is arranged only to avoid crossing branches.

AnnotatedAnnotated, seed filtered




























Girvan-Newman, in its original form, does not select a stopping point from this sequence (Fortunato 2010); the removal process continues until no edges remain. A refinement published two years after the original algorithm (M. E. Newman and Girvan 2004) selects the round with the highest modularity score as the working partition, and this is the conventional choice, but it fails on this corpus: modularity continues to rise as the graph fragments, reaching its maximum only once 94.2% of nodes are singleton communities (94.3% of nodes in the seed filtered run), which is not a usable partition. This is a documented limitation of modularity on sparse networks, where it can lack a clear maximum and instead admit many different high-scoring partitions (Good, de Montjoye, and Clauset 2010). The criterion used instead counts connected components directly: the point where that count starts climbing steadily, one round after another, marks where the graph is actually breaking into pieces, independent of whether modularity happens to be rising or falling at the same time. The earliest such round is 9,312 (Annotated) and 8,700 (Annotated, seed filtered), and it is used for every community grouping in the rest of this document.

This section identifies each cluster’s most-cited papers by within-cluster citation degree, then has a language model write a label and description from their titles, independent of the F1 annotation codebook. Comparing these labels against the codebook happens separately, in 03_joined_descriptions.qmd.
For each cluster, select_representatives.py ranks the cluster’s own papers by how many other members of that cluster cite them, and takes the top few as a representative sample. label_clusters.py sends those titles to a language model, which sorts them into named groups and writes a label and description from the largest group; a second label is written only when a real second group exists with enough titles behind it. Full detail on both steps, including the hub-independence rule and the mechanical checks run on the model’s output, is in cluster_labelling/README.md.

The clusters can be grouped in turn. Two clusters are linked when papers in one cite papers in the other, and also when their citing papers cite many of the same works. A single run of one community-detection method is a weak basis for groups here, because the result changes with the method, the resolution and the definition of a link. The grouping below therefore runs 8 variants, with 5 random seeds each, on every cluster of every size. The variants are Leiden at four resolutions, Louvain, Infomap on undirected and on directed links, and Leiden on shared references. Two clusters share a group when they were grouped together in at least 50% of the runs on average. A cluster forms a group alone when no other cluster meets that test with it, which means the variants disagree about which cluster it belongs with. Each group reports the share of runs in which its members stayed together. A high share is necessary but not enough, because weakly linked clusters can be grouped together consistently without sharing a theme, so the cluster labels in each row need reading as well.

title: Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions
text:
The partition plots above use the Fruchterman-Reingold layout (fr, 500 iterations, with igraph’s grid speed-up). The layouts below were tried and are kept for reference with eval: false. Each calls the same plotting function as the main plots, so any of them can be switched on one at a time and run on either graph.

fr spreads the papers that cite a hub around it, so each community reads as a region of the plot. It runs in seconds on either graph.
lgl with coolexp lowered to 0.5, the layout used before, stretches the graph into one diagonal band and leaves the highlighted communities overlapping through its middle. It is also far slower than fr on the seed-filtered graph.
drl stacks the papers that cite a hub on top of it, so every community collapses into a single dot and the plot shows nothing of its shape.
stress (graphlayouts::layout_with_stress()) is faster than drl and built to preserve graph distance. It produced a concentric-ring pattern and was rejected.
Untuned lgl places a handful of true outliers far from the rest. That is why the main plots crop the view to the 1st to 99th percentile.
lgl with repulserad doubled spread the periphery out and left the inner core dense. repulserad sets the distance at which repulsion stops acting and does not change its strength, so it is the wrong lever for core density.

The Louvain, Leiden and K-means plots, also disabled. Each saves a PNG and a PDF next to this document.

title: Part 2 — Citation graph: structural descriptions
text:
Footnotes


The proportion of possible edges that actually exist: edges present divided by every pair of nodes that could be connected. Low density is normal and expected for a citation network — most works don’t cite most other works.↩︎
A weakly connected component treats every edge as undirected: two nodes are in the same component if a path connects them in either citation direction. This is the more forgiving of the two measures here.↩︎
A strongly connected component requires an actual directed path in both directions between two nodes. Rare in citation networks, since citations are historically directed — a 2010 paper cannot cite a 2020 paper — so most strongly connected components are single isolated nodes.↩︎
A LOESS fit, not a strict linear one, to allow for a non-constant relationship across the full year range rather than forcing a single slope.↩︎

This document renders a full analysis by including each stage in sequence. It is executed through a series of included files:
The analysis also depends on a few toolsets that operate outside the Quarto render chain:

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
From seed paper to corpus
The F1 corpus is built from the bibliography of the seed paper (Lund & Sindbæk 2022): its cited references, treated as a first generation of descendant works. The seed paper’s own reference list resolves to 576 works in the bibliography; the F1 corpus analyzed here holds 369, meaning 207 references were excluded.

Selection criteria
Two exclusion criteria were applied when building the F1 set from the seed paper’s reference list:

Full books and edited volumes with consolidated bibliographies. A book’s reference list is not comparable in scale or character to a journal article’s, and including it as a single node alongside articles would distort network measures, centrality in particular, that depend on reference-list size.
Methodological/technical reports outside the study’s interpretive scope, judged case by case. One paper (Cannell et al. 2016, a geochemical pXRF methods chapter in an edited excavation volume) was excluded on this basis; it remains in the wider bibliography as a citation target for the papers that cite it, but was removed from the annotated F1 seed set.

No other structured record of exclusion reasons for the remaining works in the seed’s reference list currently exists; this count has not yet been individually itemized and categorized beyond these two documented criteria.

title: BibVik Citation Analysis: Camps, Communities, and Citational Politics
text:
From detection to resolved bibliography
The citation graph is built in two stages: automated detection of candidate citations per paper, then manual correction and deduplication across the whole bibliography.



Raw citation detections by method, before merging duplicate detections of the same citation


Detection method
Raw detections




Structured reference list (GROBID)
24560


Inline citation markers
17754


LLM body-text scan
11487


Text-pattern matching
10538


LLM bibliography reparse
1671


LLM footnote scan
673





Each paper’s PDF is scanned by six independent methods: GROBID parsing its structured reference list, matching inline citation markers in the body text, text-pattern matching, and three LLM-based passes (a body-text scan, a bibliography reparse, and a footnote scan). A single real citation is frequently flagged by more than one method. The 66,683 raw detections above merge down to 31,994 deduplicated citations per-paper, which are then carried into the bibliography-wide correction process below. The structured reference list and inline-marker matching account for the large majority of raw detections; the LLM-based methods contribute the remainder, recovering citations the structured parser misses, most commonly footnote-embedded references and citations in non-standard or non-Latin formats. 1.16% of bibliography entries (167) have no title recorded: a paper in the corpus cites them, but the entry itself has no title or an incomplete author.
Once detected, citations are carried into a single shared bibliography, where the same underlying work can be independently detected from multiple citing papers and needs consolidating into one record. This consolidation, along with other manual corrections, is tracked in a running corrections file (corrections.yaml) rather than as edits to the raw pipeline output.



Manual, individually-reasoned correction actions applied to the bibliography (corrections.yaml)






Action
Count




set (field corrections: author, year, title, citer lists, etc.)
17528


delete (fabricated or unresolvable ghost entries removed)
1770


create (missing entries added from manually verified source data)
960


merge (duplicate entries combined)
396


reject (candidate merges/matches checked and confirmed distinct)
80


split (single entries separated into multiple genuine works)
19





Two bulk, mechanical field backfills are tracked in the same file but excluded from the table above: a language value was set on 12,807 entries and a detection value on 12,804 entries, both copied wholesale from the pipeline’s own processing cache rather than individually reasoned. Combined they account for more set actions than every other correction in the file put together, so are reported separately to avoid making the file’s manual-correction volume look larger than it is.
As of this writing the file holds 20753 individually-reasoned correction actions, plus the 25,611 bulk field backfills noted above. The great majority of delete actions removed “ghost” entries: records with no title and no raw citation text, produced when the extraction pipeline generated a placeholder entry it was never able to resolve to a real source. merge actions consolidated cases where the same underlying work had been independently created under two or more citekeys, most commonly because one version came from an automated reference-list extraction with no linked PDF and a second, fuller version was later created when the paper’s own PDF was located and processed directly, or because the same source was independently extracted from two different citing papers’ reference lists, the cross-paper duplication this section exists to resolve. set actions in the table above cover routine field-level corrections: fixing fabricated or garbled author names, correcting mis-parsed years and titles, and adding real citation relationships (cited_by entries) that automated detection missed or failed to resolve on the first pass.
One deletion in this file was subsequently confirmed incorrect and reversed: a genuine F1 paper had been marked fabricated across multiple earlier review passes despite being a real, verifiable source, and was restored with corrected metadata once checked directly against its source PDF. This is noted here as a reminder that delete corrections, like any other, should be treated as provisional until checked against a primary source rather than as settled fact on the strength of a confident-sounding note.
